title: The poor
hookLine: a soldier cuts his cloak in half at a cold gate: Martin of Tours, Matthew 25, and Christ met in the poor
tomorrow: why do some Hindus say sorry to the floor each morning?

cards: A clipboard, a line of people, and the easy move is to hand over a form and call the next name. Many paths ask something for the poor. Here's one answer, from a city gate in Roman Gaul in a hard winter.
A young soldier named Martin rides up to Amiens. A man sits at the gate with almost nothing on, begging, and one person after another walks past him. Martin has no money with him.
Only his weapons and his soldier's cloak. He draws his sword.

teach.b: He cuts the cloak in two, gives one half to the man, and wraps himself in what's left. Some of the people watching laugh at how he looks. That's from the Life of Martin by Sulpicius Severus, a writer who knew him.
Martin dreams of Christ, wearing the half-cloak, telling the angels around him that Martin clothed him with it. And Martin wasn't even baptized yet. The dream is a parable come to life.

teach.h: DONE TO THE LEAST, DONE TO ME.
teach.b: In Matthew 25, the king tells the people who fed and clothed and visited: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me."
That's the Christian teaching under the whole story: Christ is met in the poor.
From that chapter come the works of mercy: feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, welcome the stranger, clothe the naked, visit the sick and the prisoner.
So the poor, in this teaching, aren't a cause handled from far away. They're where Christ waits to be clothed. And Martin didn't send help through someone else.
He handed it over himself, face to face, at the gate.

how: Christians practice the works of mercy drawn from Matthew 25 through parish food pantries, coat drives, and visits to the sick and to prisons. Martin of Tours is honored as a saint, and his cloak story is retold on his feast day.

games.q: a coworker is collecting coats for a shelter. you own one warm coat and one worn-out one. what does Martin's story point to?
o: give something real, even if it costs you a little

games.why: Martin had nothing spare: he cut his own cloak in half. the story isn't about leftovers; it's about meeting Christ in the one in front of you.

practice: Rest one hand on something you're wearing, a sleeve or a coat, and feel how it keeps you warm. Then bring to mind one person in need you're likely to pass this week.
Let the breath settle while you choose one thing you could give them, face to face.

wordCard.voice: The poor: in Christian teaching, the least of these, the ones Christ says he is met in. Martin met him at a cold gate.
